reason: The learning target is auditory and temporal: the learner must hear a da-DUM pulse and then attach the names iamb and pentameter to what they already hear. A visual animation of stress marks would substitute typography for the skill being taught, and it would encourage the very error the case warns about, treating the marks as an abstract pattern that can be counted off a picture. Ten syllables is a visual count; five iambs is an audible one. The case also asks for an audio alternative and a text-only fallback, which a static scansion sheet supplies directly, whereas an animated scene would need that fallback anyway and add nothing the recording does not already do.
staticAlternative: A read-aloud scansion sheet. The teacher reads the line twice, once naturally and once while clapping on each stress, then hands out the line printed in large type with the scansion already pencilled in: ˘ and ´ over every syllable and a thin vertical bar between the five feet, with a margin count of 5 feet and 10 syllables. Beside it sits a contrast line in trochaic pentameter, same ten syllables and opposite stress pattern, so the learner can see that syllable count alone does not decide the metre. Then a blank third line for the learner to mark from the recording, checked against a key that names any foot that is arguable, plus one written question, 'which word does the fourth stress land on, and what does that emphasis do to the sense?', answered in a sentence. The whole exercise works silently from the marked sheet and the printed key when audio is unavailable.
